catalog_quote: 1.1. Stress. Within words, primary stress is generally predictable. Secondary stress is noted in longer utterances, but has not been analyzed. ... 2.21. Stress placement. A CVC root is the base of most Spokan words. These may occur alone or take prefixes and suffixes. Suffixed forms may take primary stress on a suffix or on the root. The roots and suffixes involved will determine stress placement. Suffixes fall into three groups: those that are inherently-stressed (suffixes which always take the stress from a root); unstressed suffixes, which do not have an underlying vowel; and variable-stress suffixes, which have both stressed and unstressed variants. The last take stress when it is not automatically placed on the root or on an inherently-stressed suffix in the same form. When unstressed, their underlying vowel is lost. sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for Spokane: Carlson 1989 'Reduplication and Stress in Spokane' (IJAL 55(2): 204-213, doi 10.1086/466113), already in our per-language bibliography. It is squarely about Spokane word stress but is paywalled: the publisher site blocks our network (not reachable by automated download on landing and PDF), Crossref carries no license, OpenAlex's 'OA' pointer is just the WALS RefDB metadata record, archive. No first-hand text was read, so the best new statement is not found. Its content is known second-hand from the open Bates & Carlson WPLC paper held by the project (sec. 2.1, p. 75), which states that Carlson 1989 shows 'stress is morphologically determined' via the hierarchy strong suffixes > strong roots > variable suffixes > weak roots > weak suffixes, prefixes unstressed, no secondary stress; this matches the catalog's 'morphological' coding from Carlson 1972 (and the already-read 1990/1991 ICSNL updates), so nothing in this search of works with stress in the title contradicts the catalog. Priority for acquiring Carlson 1989: medium (peer-reviewed statement of record and StressTyp2's cited source, but its rule is already documented first-hand from Carlson 1972 and the 1990/1991 Carlson & Bates papers); Harvard has online access via the Harvard library catalogue. download attempts and metadata records with stamp).

new_statements.quote: Stress. Words built on this inventory are based on typical CVC(C) roots with an extensive range of prefixes, suffixes and infixes. Four reduplication patterns, and a complex system of affixes with root-like meanings, combine to create polysynthetic words (Carlson 1989, 1990). Each word has one main stress, determined by a complex interrelationship between the phonology and the morphological stress-classes of constituent morphemes (Black 1996). Phonological processes delete unstressed vowels; consonant strings that result undergo further reductions (Carlson 1972). [p. 97:] Montana Salish also typically shortens words by eliminating all phonological material following the stressed vowel.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's qs-tier record (Carlson 1972 + Bates & Carlson WPLC) codes Spokane as set by morphology: one primary stress per word assigned by morpheme stress class (strong suffixes > strong roots > variable suffixes > weak roots), prefixes unstressed, unstressed vowels deleted. Carlson & Esling's 'one main stress, determined by.. the morphological stress-classes of constituent morphemes.. Phonological processes delete unstressed vowels' is the same analysis in summary form; it adds no hierarchy, weight or secondary-stress detail. new_statements.rule_in_words: One main (culminative) stress per word; its position is not phonologically fixed but falls out of the morphological stress-classes of the morphemes in the word (root and suffix classes) interacting with the phonology; vowels that end up unstressed are deleted. The article gives no placement hierarchy itself and defers to Black 1996 for it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (the section speaks only of 'one main stress').
new_statements.identity_note: Carlson & Esling 2000 treat Spokane, Kalispel and Montana Salish (Flathead) as 'nearly identical dialects of an Interior Salish language'; their data come from one Kalispel speaker (Alex Sherwood) and two Spokane speakers (Margaret Sherwood, Pauline Flett), recorded 1969, 1972 and 1992. They remark that Montana Salish 'typically shortens words by eliminating all phonological material following the stressed vowel', a dialect difference in post-tonic truncation, not in stress placement. The stress statement is given for the language as a whole.

sources.quote: [second-hand, Bates & Carlson WPLC p. 75:] Carlson (1989) summarizes previous work on Spokane stress (Carlson (1972, 1980)), illustrating that stress is morphologically determined. Root and suffix morphemes fall into classes which form a stress hierarchy: (1) strong suffixes / strong roots / variable suffixes / weak roots / weak suffixes. When morphemes are combined to form words, stress falls on that morpheme which bears the features of the highest place in the stress hierarchy. ... Spokane is typical among Salishan languages in that prefixes are unstressed, but unlike some related languages in having no secondary stress.
